beats.title: A Visual Overhaul of the Static Teleportation Effect
beats.body: The Aleph One open-source Marathon engine renders a 'static' visual effect when characters teleport in or out. The existing shader produced what contributors described as a grey haze — smooth and diffuse. A collaborator proposed replacing it with a blockier, more pixelated version intended to more closely evoke the look of the original classic game. The change touched a single shader file and was accompanied by screenshots showing the new chunky, tile-like static pattern alongside bloom (glow) support that the old shader could not achieve.

beats.title: Ship It as Default or Relegate It to a Plugin?
beats.body: The core tension was whether this new visual style should become the default experience for all players or be offered as an optional plugin. Three overlapping concerns drove the debate. First, the block size was fixed and did not scale with screen resolution, making the effect look dramatically different — and arguably broken — at low or high resolutions. Second, the new shader relied on GPU features and random-number generation approaches that caused visible glitches on some hardware, including color banding, full-screen white flashes, and stripes that worsened over time as the elapsed-time value grew large. Third, shipping it as the default would remove the original effect entirely, leaving no recourse for players who preferred the classic look or whose hardware could not render the new one correctly.

beats.title: Position A — treellama
beats.body: treellama appreciated the aesthetic of the new effect but raised practical objections to making it the default. At lower resolutions the block count dropped so dramatically that the effect lost all sense of randomness and looked obviously wrong. At 1080p it was already too coarse. More importantly, shipping it as the default would eliminate the original shader entirely, with no fallback for purists or for players on hardware that could not render the new version correctly. treellama's preferred resolution was to move the new effect into a plugin bundled with the default data files, preserving the original behavior for everyone else while still making the new look readily available.
beats.author: treellama

beats.title: Position B — TrajansRow
beats.body: TrajansRow, the author of the change, agreed in principle that moving to a plugin was acceptable, but pushed back on the framing that the effect was simply broken. The intent was fidelity to the original game's look, and the block size was an acknowledged approximation that could be improved by exposing the screen resolution to the shader as a uniform value, allowing the effect to scale properly. On the hardware-compatibility front, TrajansRow investigated each reported failure, traced the white-flash and stripe problems to how large elapsed-time values were handled by certain GPUs, and proposed targeted fixes rather than a full revert. The position was that the underlying approach was sound and worth refining rather than abandoning.
beats.author: TrajansRow

beats.question: Given that the new effect looks better on some setups but breaks on others, and that its block size does not adapt to resolution, would you merge it as the new default, hold it until the scaling and compatibility issues are resolved, or ship it only as an opt-in plugin? What criteria would you use to decide, and who bears the cost of each choice?

beats.title: Merged as Default in January 2019
beats.body: The pull request was merged on January 26, 2019, making the blockier static effect the new default behavior rather than a plugin. The merge happened relatively early in the discussion timeline — before the resolution and hardware-compatibility concerns were fully surfaced and debated in the later comments, which continued into March 2019. The commit history shows the author iterated on bloom intensity and block size in the days immediately following the initial proposal, and those refinements were what landed. The subsequent discussion about GPU glitches, large time-value overflow, and resolution scaling represents follow-on investigation after the change was already in the main branch.

beats.title: Engineering Lessons
lessons: Resolution-dependent visual effects need to be tested across the full range of supported resolutions before merging, because a fixed scale that looks intentional at one resolution can look completely broken at another — and this is not always obvious from a single screenshot.

Shader compatibility across GPU vendors and driver versions is notoriously uneven; effects that rely on precise floating-point behavior or large accumulated time values should be stress-tested on diverse hardware before being promoted to the default experience.

When a change removes an existing behavior entirely, the cost falls on every user who preferred or depended on that behavior — offering the new approach as an opt-in plugin first lets the community validate it without that risk, and is a lower-stakes path to eventual promotion as the default.
